forecast.session_note: Pre-event note for the week of 5-9 Oct 2026. Backdrop: the Fed is in a hiking cycle under Chair Warsh (25bp to 3.75-4.00% on 16 Sep, 12-0, median dot showing one more 2026 hike), but October hike pricing collapsed last week (Kalshi ~17% hike / 84% hold for 28 Oct; CME-based trackers ~77-82% hold) after Williams and Jefferson signalled no urgency, core PCE for August came in at 0.2% m/m and 3.0% y/y (below consensus) and September payrolls printed +29K with unemployment at 4.2%. December is now the market's hike vehicle (~70% odds of a 2026 hike). Despite that dovish repricing the dollar is at 2026 highs (DXY 102.08, RSI 74.6, highest since April 2025) on oil-driven euro weakness, with EUR/USD at 1.1225 (RSI 20.9, bottom of the 20d range) and GBP/USD at 1.3201. BoJ has hiked to 1.25% (18 Sep, 7-2); the 1 Oct Summary of Opinions disappointed October-hike hopes and pushed USD/JPY to 158.44, but a 5 Oct Japan Times sources story says the BoJ may conclude underlying inflation has reached ~2%. The week's biggest two-sided risks are Ueda tomorrow (yen-positive surprise least priced) and the UoM inflation expectations print (the de-anchoring metric Warsh is watching). Scoreboard from the last cycle is mixed: 2 hits, 2 misses, 3 unclear.

forecasts.event: US ISM Services PMI, September 2026 (ISM, 10:00 ET / 14:00 GMT, 5 Oct)

evidence.fact: S&P Global flash US services PMI jumped to 58.7 in September from 56.8 in August, with the composite at 58.4, the fastest output growth in over five years and payroll growth the strongest since 2022 (S&P Global, 23 Sep).

ISM Manufacturing PMI for the same month printed 54.5, only 0.1pt below August and essentially flat, i.e. no September deceleration in the ISM family (ISM, 1 Oct) — but it still missed its 54.8 consensus despite the parallel S&P flash manufacturing surge to 57.0, a direct warning against extrapolating the S&P flash into ISM.
August ISM Services beat by over a point (55.4 vs 54.1-54.3 consensus) with business activity 61.7 and new orders 60.9, both above 60 — strong momentum into September (ISM/TD Economics).

ISM Services employment index has contracted for two straight months (47.8 in August) and September non-farm payrolls were just +29K with services hiring soft, a persistent drag on the headline composite.
Consensus at 55.1 embeds a mild deceleration from 55.4 that little September survey evidence corroborates.

forecasts.lean_rationale: Business-survey evidence for September is uniformly firm (S&P composite at a five-year high, ISM manufacturing flat rather than slowing), so the small deceleration embedded in 55.1 looks more likely to be undershot than overshot. The offset is real: the ISM services employment sub-index is still below 50 and the manufacturing analogue missed its consensus, which is why conviction is limited.
forecasts.confidence_reason: The strongest single read-across (same-month ISM manufacturing) contradicted the S&P flash signal, and the employment component is a live drag; the evidence tilts but does not separate cleanly.
forecasts.whats_priced: The dollar is at 2026 highs with only ~17-20% priced for an October hike and roughly 70% for a hike by December, so the market is already assuming the US growth side stays firm while the Fed waits. After Friday's +29K payrolls, a solid services print is treated as the thing that keeps December alive rather than as news about October. The prices-paid sub-index (72.6 in August, fifth 70+ reading in six months) is the line most likely to be traded.
forecasts.asymmetry: Skewed toward a downside surprise mattering more. A beat largely confirms what the S&P flash already advertised and runs into stretched positioning (DXY RSI 74.6, EUR/USD RSI 20.9 at the 20d low of 1.1225), so follow-through could be limited. A sub-54 print with employment deeper in contraction would stack on the payrolls miss and is the less-priced tail.

reactions.if_outcome: Headline above ~56 with prices paid holding above 70
reactions.then_currency: would likely support the dollar by firming December hike pricing, with EUR/USD pressured against the 1.1225 range low

reactions.if_outcome: Headline in the 54.5-55.5 area, prices paid little changed
reactions.then_currency: likely a muted reaction inside the ~0.27% 1SD daily range for EUR/USD, with attention shifting to Wednesday's minutes

reactions.if_outcome: Headline below 54 with employment weaker than 47.8
reactions.then_currency: would likely weigh on the dollar given freshly sensitised labour-market concerns, with EUR/USD scope to unwind back toward the mid-1.13s and USD/JPY to retreat from the 158.46 200-day

forecasts.event: BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda speaks (06:35 GMT / 15:35 JST, 6 Oct)
forecasts.consensus: No numeric consensus. Benchmark: a reiteration of gradual, data-dependent hikes with no commitment on the 30 Oct meeting. Read 'above consensus' as hawkish relative to that (keeping October live / explicitly endorsing that underlying inflation has reached 2%), 'below consensus' as dovish.

evidence.fact: Japan Times reported on 5 Oct, citing sources, that the BoJ is considering concluding that underlying inflation has reached around 2% — a judgement that would logically accompany the 30 Oct Outlook Report and further hikes.
Tokyo CPI rose 2.7% in September, the fastest since late 2025 and the first break above 2% since December 2025, as subsidies lapsed (Japan Times, 2 Oct).
At the September MPM the board hiked to 1.25% (7-2) only three months after the June move, and Ueda framed it as a new phase focused on preventing an overshoot rather than coaxing inflation up.

The 1 Oct Summary of Opinions disappointed October-hike expectations; Japanese rate markets scaled back tightening pricing and USD/JPY rose to 158.44, with MUFG and Citi both pointing to December (MUFG/FXStreet, 1 Oct).

The yen is weak at 157.67 after official intervention episodes earlier in 2026 and a July rate check, which raises the political incentive for firm language; ex-BoJ official Momma puts October hike odds at only 20-30% (Japan Times, 28 Sep).

forecasts.lean_rationale: The flow of official and semi-official signalling in the last week — Tokyo CPI at 2.7%, the sources story on declaring underlying inflation at 2%, and the September hike framed as overshoot prevention — tilts the risk toward Ueda sounding firmer than the post-Summary-of-Opinions market read, even if he stops short of pre-committing to 30 October.
forecasts.confidence_reason: The venue and text are unconfirmed, Ueda habitually avoids pre-commitment, and the most recent official communication (Summary of Opinions) cut the other way.
forecasts.whats_priced: Markets have largely taken 30 October off the table and moved the hike to December after the Summary of Opinions; USD/JPY at 157.67 sits just under the 200-day at 158.46 and below the 20d high of 158.85, with carry still heavily in the dollar's favour against a 1.25% policy rate.
forecasts.asymmetry: Lopsided toward yen strength. Because an October move is mostly priced out, hawkish signalling (keeping October live, blessing the 'underlying inflation at 2%' conclusion) has far more room to move JPY than dovish repetition, which is the base case already in the price. Upside in USD/JPY is additionally capped by the 158.46/158.85 zone and by intervention risk after this year's episodes; the 1SD day is ±0.57%, so a repricing of 30 October would be a multi-sigma event.

reactions.if_outcome: Ueda explicitly says underlying inflation is at or around 2%, or declines to rule out an October move
reactions.then_currency: would likely support the yen, with USD/JPY pressured back from the 158.46 200-day toward the lower half of the 153.27-158.85 range

reactions.if_outcome: Standard gradualist language, data-dependence, no October signal
reactions.then_currency: likely leaves USD/JPY driven by US yields, with the 200-day at 158.46 the immediate reference

reactions.if_outcome: Emphasis on downside risks from energy costs, overseas growth or the need to see wage data before moving again
reactions.then_currency: would likely weigh on the yen, though gains above 158.85 would run into intervention risk

forecasts.event: FOMC minutes of the 15-16 September 2026 meeting (14:00 ET / 18:00 GMT, 7 Oct)
forecasts.consensus: No numeric consensus. Benchmark: minutes consistent with a unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75-4.00%, broad concern about inflation at 3% core PCE and a strong majority seeing one more 2026 hike. 'Above consensus' = more hawkish than that (urgency about back-to-back moves, de-anchoring worries); 'below consensus' = more conditional/patient than the SEP implied.

evidence.fact: The September decision was unanimous (12-0) with the median dot showing one further 2026 hike, and Warsh's press conference stressed inflation is too high while offering limited forward guidance (Federal Reserve transcript, 16 Sep; KPMG; Chase).

The minutes pre-date the two prints that caused last week's dovish repricing: August core PCE at 0.2% m/m and 3.0% y/y (below the 0.3%/3.3% expected, 30 Sep) and September payrolls at +29K with unemployment up to 4.2% (BLS, 2 Oct).

Since the meeting, Williams and Jefferson have made an unusually clear case against a back-to-back October hike (Reuters, 1 Oct), while Barr leaned hawkish on 23 Sep — the committee is visibly split, so the minutes can plausibly furnish quotes for either side.

Inflation-related sub-indices remain hot (ISM manufacturing prices 77.9 in September, near the March war peak of 78.3; ISM services prices 72.6 in August), so a section on inflation-expectation risks would read hawkish against ~17-20% October pricing.
Warsh has run shorter, lower-guidance communications since taking the chair, which argues for minutes with less exploitable detail than usual.

forecasts.lean_rationale: The hawkish skeleton — unanimous hike, one more dot, inflation too high — is already public from the statement, SEP and press conference, and the incremental content (how many wanted to pause, how the labour-market downside was discussed) is genuinely two-sided. The minutes are also stale relative to the soft core PCE and payrolls that drove last week's repricing.
forecasts.confidence_reason: No directional evidence separates from the already-published September communications, and the market's framework has moved on from that meeting.
forecasts.whats_priced: October is priced close to a hold (Kalshi 84% hold / 17% hike; futures trackers 77-82% hold), with a 2026 hike still around 70% via December. The dollar nonetheless sits at 2026 highs (DXY 102.08), so the price action is being driven more by oil, euro weakness and US growth outperformance than by near-term Fed pricing.
forecasts.asymmetry: The hawkish side is the less-priced one. With only ~17-20% in for October, language showing that many participants judged further tightening likely to be needed soon, or that they were worried about inflation expectations de-anchoring, would be the bigger mover. Dovish detail largely restates what Williams and Jefferson said last week and should be close to a non-event — though it could help an overbought dollar correct, with EUR/USD RSI at 20.9 and DXY RSI at 74.6 leaving the pain trade on the dollar-negative side.

reactions.if_outcome: Minutes show a broad majority leaning toward another hike 'soon' and prominent concern about inflation expectations
reactions.then_currency: would likely support the dollar via firmer December pricing, keeping EUR/USD pinned near the 1.1225 range low

reactions.if_outcome: Minutes read as a cautious, conditional hike with visible discussion of labour-market downside
reactions.then_currency: would likely weigh modestly on the dollar, with scope for a stretched DXY to unwind from the top of its 98.61-102.08 range

reactions.if_outcome: Short, low-detail minutes consistent with Warsh's pared-back communications
reactions.then_currency: likely a muted FX reaction well inside the ±0.27% 1SD day for EUR/USD

forecasts.event: US initial jobless claims, week ending 3 October 2026 (DoL, 08:30 ET / 12:30 GMT, 8 Oct)

evidence.fact: Claims have been below 200K for three consecutive weeks (196K, 198K, 197K), with the four-week average down to 200K and continuing claims at 1.701m, the lowest since March 2023 (DoL/FRED, 1 Oct).
Consensus has over-forecast claims repeatedly in recent weeks: 208K expected vs 196K actual, 201K vs 198K, 200K vs 197K.

The September employment report showed weakness via hiring, not firing (+29K payrolls but no layoff surge; the unemployment rate rose to 4.2% mainly on labour-force entry per CNBC/BLS) — consistent with claims staying historically low.
After a 'lowest since July' print, weekly mean reversion plus early-October seasonal-factor noise argue for a bounce back toward the 200K area.
The gap between consensus and recent actuals is only 2-4K, well inside normal weekly noise.

forecasts.lean_rationale: The run rate (196-198K for three weeks), a four-week average at 200K and a consistent pattern of consensus sitting above the actual tilt the odds slightly toward another sub-200K print, but the margin involved is a few thousand claims — statistically trivial.
forecasts.confidence_reason: The implied edge is smaller than the series' weekly standard error, and seasonal factors around the start of October add noise.
forecasts.whats_priced: Claims near 57-year lows are the market's main evidence that the labour market is cooling through hiring rather than layoffs — the benign interpretation that underpins the 'Fed can wait, not cut' setup and a 2026-high dollar. A print in the 190-210K band is effectively already in the price.
forecasts.asymmetry: Clearly skewed. Another sub-200K print confirms the consensus story and should barely register. A jump above roughly 210-215K would land on a market freshly sensitised by Friday's +29K payrolls and 4.2% unemployment rate, and would be the bigger move by some distance, because almost nothing of that scenario is discounted.

reactions.if_outcome: Claims below ~195K with continuing claims falling again
reactions.then_currency: would mildly support the dollar, but likely inside the ±0.27% 1SD day for EUR/USD

reactions.if_outcome: Claims above ~212K, or a clear jump in continuing claims off the 1.70m low
reactions.then_currency: would likely weigh on the dollar by reviving labour-market concerns and trimming December hike odds, with EUR/USD scope to rebound off 1.1225

forecasts.event: University of Michigan preliminary consumer sentiment, October 2026 (10:00 ET / 14:00 GMT, 9 Oct)

evidence.fact: Pump prices have turned down from a record: AAA's national average fell nearly 7 cents in the week to 1 Oct to $4.41 and was $4.37 on 4 Oct, after a record September monthly average of $4.33; crude is ~$90, about 3% lower over the past month.
The September employment report (+29K payrolls, unemployment up to 4.2%) landed on 2 October, inside the early-October survey window, and headline coverage was uniformly negative.
The series has badly undershot consensus recently: September preliminary came in at 47.8 against 51.0 expected, a four-month low, with expectations down 10.1% to 46.3 (UoM/Trading Economics).
Sentiment is already near historic lows (48.1 final September, 12.7% below a year earlier), which mechanically limits further downside and has historically produced small bounces when gasoline falls.
UoM cited rekindled trade disputes alongside high prices as the September drag; those have not visibly resolved.

forecasts.lean_rationale: Two medium-weight signals point in opposite directions: falling pump prices, which is the single most reliable driver of this series, against a weak jobs report inside the survey window plus a demonstrated recent tendency to undershoot forecasts. Neither dominates.
forecasts.confidence_reason: Offsetting drivers of similar weight, and a series that has swung 3-4 points against consensus in each of the last two months.
forecasts.whats_priced: Very little. The market has stopped trading the sentiment headline per se — it is already at crisis-era levels and the dollar is at 2026 highs regardless. What is priced is the narrative that the US consumer is squeezed but the Fed is still inflation-focused.
forecasts.asymmetry: The larger move sits with a sharply weaker print (say below 46) that would stack onto the payrolls miss and make the consumer-weakness story harder to ignore ahead of the 28 October meeting — a dollar-negative tail. A modest beat, which the gasoline decline makes plausible, is unlikely to generate more than noise. In both cases the inflation-expectations component released alongside is likely to dominate the FX reaction.

reactions.if_outcome: Headline above ~49 alongside stable or lower inflation expectations
reactions.then_currency: would likely offer mild dollar support, though within the ±0.27% 1SD day
likely a non-event for FX, with the inflation-expectations line driving any move

reactions.if_outcome: Headline below ~46 with the expectations index making new lows
reactions.then_currency: would likely weigh on the dollar, giving an overbought DXY (RSI 74.6) a reason to correct from the top of its 98.61-102.08 range

forecasts.event: University of Michigan preliminary year-ahead inflation expectations, October 2026 (10:00 ET / 14:00 GMT, 9 Oct)
forecasts.consensus: No published consensus; benchmark is unchanged at the previous 4.6% (September, the highest since June and up from 3.4% before the Iran conflict)

evidence.fact: Year-ahead expectations in this survey track pump prices closely, and AAA's national average has fallen from a record September monthly average of $4.33 to $4.41 on 1 Oct (-7c w/w) and $4.37 on 4 Oct, with crude around $90 and down ~3% on the month.
August core PCE surprised lower at 0.2% m/m and 3.0% y/y (vs 0.3%/3.3% expected, BEA 30 Sep), and core CPI slowed to 2.4% y/y in August from 2.5%.

Business-survey price pressures remain intense — ISM manufacturing prices 77.9 in September (near the March war peak) and ISM services prices 72.6 in August — and UoM respondents cited rekindled trade disputes in September.
Gasoline is still near record levels in absolute terms, and consumers anchor on levels as well as changes; the September jump to 4.6% came with explicit references to fuel costs.
The series is highly volatile this year (3.8% in March to 4.7%, back down, then 4.6% in September), so 0.2-0.3pt swings in either direction are routine.

forecasts.lean_rationale: The main mechanical driver — pump prices — turned down inside the survey window for the first time since the summer, which more often than not produces at least a tick lower in the one-year series. Working the other way are still-record price levels, hot ISM price indices and renewed trade friction, so the expected move is small and could easily be swamped by the series' own volatility.
forecasts.confidence_reason: The implied edge is roughly 0.1-0.2pt against a series that routinely moves 0.3pt on noise, and the level-versus-change tension in consumer perceptions is unresolved.
forecasts.whats_priced: This is the de-anchoring metric Chair Warsh has pointed to, and with October a near-hold and December roughly 70% priced for a hike, the market is implicitly assuming expectations stay elevated but do not accelerate. A stable 4.5-4.7% is fully in the price.
forecasts.asymmetry: The hawkish tail is the more powerful one. A move to 4.8% or above would be read as evidence of de-anchoring, re-arming the December hike case and potentially putting October back in play — the single largest dollar-positive surprise on this week's calendar. A fall toward 4.3-4.4% mainly confirms the dovish repricing that already happened last week, so its dollar-negative impact should be smaller.

reactions.if_outcome: Year-ahead expectations at 4.8% or higher, especially with long-run expectations rising
reactions.then_currency: would likely support the dollar via renewed December (and residual October) hike pricing, with EUR/USD pressed against the 1.1225 range low and USD/JPY toward the 158.46 200-day
likely a limited FX reaction, leaving the dollar driven by oil and the Fed-speak calendar

reactions.if_outcome: Expectations falling to 4.4% or below alongside a weak sentiment headline
reactions.then_currency: would likely weigh on the dollar, with an overbought DXY vulnerable to a pullback from 102.08 toward the middle of its 20-day range

resolutions.actual: 1.5% q/q annualised (BEA second estimate, 26 Aug 2026; 1.48% unrounded, revised down 0.02pt from the advance estimate)
resolutions.note: Printed exactly in line with the 1.5% consensus, so the 'below consensus' lean neither hit nor missed at the rounded headline — the unrounded 0.02pt downward revision is not a scoreable surprise. Worth recording that the direction later went the other way: BEA's third estimate on 30 Sep revised Q2 up sharply to 2.2%, with Q1 lifted to 2.5%.
Our 'above consensus' lean at medium confidence was wrong — the index fell a full point and undershot consensus by 0.6. New orders fell to 53.7 from 56.7; prices stayed at 71.1. A clear scoring loss.

resolutions.actual: 2.4% y/y core (HICP ex energy, food, alcohol & tobacco), down from 2.5% (Eurostat flash, 1 Sep 2026)
resolutions.note: Consensus was 2.5% and our lean was 'in line'; the flash came in a tenth below. Narrow, but it printed off consensus on the downside, so scoring it as a miss rather than unclear. Headline HICP meanwhile jumped to 3.3% on a 14.3% y/y energy rate.

The 'no clear lean' call is unscoreable by construction. For the record the print was a very large upside surprise — roughly triple consensus — so the low-confidence agnostic stance cost us a strong signal, even if it was not a wrong call. Note the August figure was subsequently revised down in the 2 Oct report.

resolutions.actual: +0.3% m/m (BLS; confirmed in the Real Earnings release for August 2026, 11 Sep)
resolutions.note: Consensus 0.3%, lean 'in line', printed 0.3%. Scoring this as a hit because the lean explicitly called an in-line print; real average hourly earnings fell 0.1% m/m as CPI outpaced wages.
Consensus 4.1%, lean 'in line', printed 4.1% unchanged. Same scoring convention as AHE: an explicit in-line call that printed in line. (It has since risen to 4.2% in the September report.)

resolutions.actual: Keynote 'The institutional form of independent central banks: from history to contemporary challenges', LSE TRIUM Anniversary Conference, published 4 Sep 2026
resolutions.note: The speech was exactly the structural, institutional benchmark described — central bank independence, accountability and legitimacy — with no near-term policy signal on the 17 September decision. The 'no clear lean' call was unscoreable but the characterisation of the event was correct.
